items.q: Type an expression for the number of ways to line up 5 different books on a shelf, and check its value.

mistakes.why: That counts only the first two places. All five places are filled: 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 5!.
Once a book is placed it cannot be used again, so the choices go down: 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.

options: That is $4^2$, not the factorial.
Right: $4! = 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24$.

items.q: A quiz has 10 questions. Type an expression for the number of ways to choose which 3 questions a student gets right.

mistakes.why: That counts ordered choices. Which 3 questions are right does not depend on order, so divide by 3! = 6: 10C3.
Choosing 3 of 10 is not 10 × 3. Use the combination 10C3.

items.q: How many different teams of 2 can be chosen from 4 people?

why.correct: A team does not depend on order: ${}_4C_2 = \frac{4 \times 3}{2 \times 1} = 6$.
options: That counts ordered pairs: Ana then Ben is the same team as Ben then Ana, so divide by 2.
That is 4 × 2, which is not how choices combine.
That is $4^2$, which allows the same person twice and counts order.

items.q: Why does choosing 3 of 10 questions use a combination and not $10 \times 9 \times 8$?

why.correct: Ordered choices overcount each set by the number of its orders. Dividing by $3!$ gives the number of sets: $\frac{720}{6} = 120$.
options: Right: $10 \times 9 \times 8 = 720$ counts each set of 3 questions $3! = 6$ times, once for each order.
Calculators handle 720 easily; the problem is counting each set several times.

items.q: A pizza shop offers 6 toppings. How many different pizzas with exactly 3 different toppings are possible?

why.correct: Order does not matter and toppings do not repeat: ${}_6C_3 = 20$.
options: That counts ordered choices; the order of toppings on a pizza does not matter.
That is 6 × 3, which is not a count of choices.
That is $6^3$, which allows the same topping three times.
Right: ${}_6C_3 = \frac{6 \times 5 \times 4}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = 20$.
